name: Digital marketing
summary: Digital marketing interviews usually mix three things: how well you know the channels (search, social, email, paid ads), whether you can read campaign numbers and act on them, and whether you can show work you've done, such as a campaign you ran or an account you grew. For many roles there is also a short task, like a campaign plan, ad copy or a website audit.
rounds: Recruiter or HR screen on your background and the channels you've worked on
Portfolio or past-work discussion: campaigns, results and what you'd change
Assignment for many roles: a campaign plan, content calendar, ad copy or an audit of a website or ad account
Hiring manager interview on channel choices, metrics and budget
Final or HR round, sometimes with a senior marketing lead
looks_for: Knowing what each channel is good for, and when not to use it
Reading metrics like click-through rate, cost per acquisition, conversion rate and return on ad spend
Linking a campaign to a business goal, not just reach or likes
Testing and learning: small tests before big budgets
Clear, persuasive writing for ads, emails and posts
Honest results: what worked, what didn't, and why

questions.text: Tell me about a campaign you ran or helped with. What was the goal, and how did it perform?
covers: The goal in one line and the audience you targeted
The channels, the rough budget size and what you tested
The result against the goal, including what fell short

questions.text: Tell me about a time a campaign underperformed. What did you do about it?
covers: How you spotted the problem in the numbers, and how early
What you changed: audience, creative, bids, landing page or timing
What you learned and now do differently

questions.text: Describe a time you worked with a designer, the sales team or a product team to get a campaign out on time.
covers: What each side needed and where you disagreed
How you agreed a brief, a timeline and who signs off
What went live and what you'd do differently next time

questions.text: Tell me about a time you had to explain marketing results to someone who only cared about sales.
covers: The number they cared about and the numbers you had
How you linked the two honestly, without overclaiming
The decision that came out of the conversation

questions.text: How would you plan the digital launch of a new product with a small budget?
covers: Clarifying the goal, the audience and what success looks like
Choosing two or three channels that fit, and saying why you'd skip others
A test-then-scale plan and the metrics you'd check each week

questions.text: Explain the difference between SEO and paid search, and when you'd rely on each.
covers: SEO builds organic traffic slowly; paid search buys visibility straight away
Cost, speed and how long the results last for each
A case where using both together makes sense

questions.text: Our cost per acquisition on paid social has doubled in a month. How would you find out why?
covers: Checking tracking and attribution first, then spend and competition changes
Breaking it down by campaign, audience, creative and placement
The fixes you'd try first and how you'd confirm they worked

questions.text: Which metrics would you report for a brand awareness campaign, and which would you leave out?
covers: Reach, frequency, video completion and branded search, plus recall studies where available
Why likes and impressions on their own can mislead
How you'd tie awareness back to a business result over time

questions.text: A landing page gets plenty of traffic but very few sign-ups. How would you improve it?
covers: Finding where people drop off, using analytics or session recordings
Testing one change at a time: headline, form length, proof, page speed
Making the page match the ad or email that sent people there

questions.text: Walk me through how you'd run an A/B test on an email subject line.
covers: One change, one main metric such as open or click rate, and a random split
Enough audience and time before you call a winner
Checking what happened after the open, such as clicks and purchases

questions.text: A brand posts regularly on Instagram or LinkedIn but gets little engagement. How would you turn that around?
covers: Auditing what's posted, who it's for and which posts have worked
A content mix and posting rhythm the team can keep up
Measuring progress by more than follower count

questions.text: What is attribution, and why can two tools report different results for the same campaign?
covers: Last-click, first-click and multi-touch models in plain words
Different tracking windows, cookies and privacy limits
Choosing one view for decisions and being clear about its limits

questions.text: How do you decide how to split a monthly budget across channels?
covers: Starting from the goal and what each channel costs per result
Keeping a small share for testing new options
Moving money based on results, and how often you'd review it

questions.text: Which marketing tools have you used, and what did you do with each one?
covers: Analytics, ads, email, social scheduling or SEO tools you've used hands-on
One concrete thing you did with each, not just the names
How you'd pick up a tool you haven't used yet

questions.text: Tell me about yourself and how you got into marketing.
covers: Your background in two or three lines
The moment or project that got you into marketing
The kind of marketing work you want to do next

questions.text: Why digital marketing, and which channel do you most want to get better at?
covers: What you enjoy about the work, shown by something you've done
One channel you want to deepen and why
How you're already learning it

questions.text: Pick a brand you follow online. What is it doing well, and what would you change?
covers: A specific brand and the channel you're talking about
One thing that works and why you think it does
One change and how you'd measure whether it helped

tips: Bring two or three campaigns you can talk through: the goal, the rough spend, the result and what you'd change.
Freshers: run something small yourself, such as a blog, a page or a tiny ad test, so you have results of your own to discuss.
Use the terms (CTR, CPC, CPA, ROAS), but explain what each number told you to do.
In a case question, ask about the goal, the audience and the budget before you pick channels.
Admit what didn't work; a failed test you can explain is a strong answer.
Free platform certifications can show a fresher knows the basics, but expect to be asked how you used what you learned.
